title: Understanding kidney stones — and getting relief
metaDescription: A practical guide from Dr. Vikram on kidney stones, symptoms, treatment options, and when to seek urology care.

hero.summary: Kidney stones are hard mineral and salt deposits that form inside your kidneys. They develop when urine becomes concentrated, allowing minerals to crystallise and stick together. With the right approach, most stones can be managed effectively.
hero.caption: Dr. Vikram · Urologist & Robotic Surgeon

paragraphs: Kidney stones are solid crystals that may form anywhere in the urinary tract. Small stones may pass naturally, but larger stones can block urine flow and cause severe pain, infection, or kidney swelling.
The exact treatment depends on stone size, location, symptoms, kidney function, infection risk, and whether the stone is moving. A urologist can match the safest option to your situation.
overview.subheading: When should you see a urologist?
subParagraphs: Seek medical care if pain is severe, fever is present, urine flow reduces, vomiting prevents hydration, or scans show a stone that is unlikely to pass.
Early evaluation helps avoid repeated emergency visits and protects kidney function.

sizeGuide.title: What your stone size means for treatment

items.copy: Very likely to pass naturally with hydration and pain medicines, if there is no infection or blockage.
May pass but could take time. Pain management and follow-up imaging are often needed.
Unlikely to pass without help. Ureteroscopy or ESWL may be considered depending on location.
Requires intervention. PCNL or ureteroscopy depends on stone burden, anatomy, and kidney health.

treatmentOptions.title: Treatment options for kidney stones
treatmentOptions.note: Note: Dr. Vikram recommends the least invasive option that can safely clear the stone.

items.title: Conservative management
items.copy: Increased fluid intake, NSAIDs for pain relief, and medicines to relax the ureter. Follow-up scans confirm whether the stone has passed.

items.title: Ureteroscopy (URS)
items.copy: A thin flexible or rigid scope is passed up the urinary tract to fragment and remove the stone without external cuts.

items.title: PCNL (Percutaneous)
items.copy: A small puncture is made in the back to access the kidney directly and clear large or complex stones.

experience.title: Dr. Vikram's experience in kidney stone
paragraphs: Dr. Vikram treats patients with kidney, ureteric, bladder, and complex recurrent stones using evidence-based and minimally invasive approaches.
The aim is not only stone clearance, but also reducing recurrence through diagnosis, dietary guidance, and follow-up planning.
subParagraphs: Modern endoscopic and laser techniques can clear many stones through natural urinary passages, reducing hospital stay and recovery time.

items.question: Do I need surgery for every kidney stone?
items.answer: No. Many small stones pass naturally. Surgery is considered when a stone is large, stuck, painful, infected, or affecting kidney function.

items.question: Which scan is best for kidney stones?
items.answer: A CT KUB is commonly used for accurate stone size and location. Ultrasound may be used for follow-up or selected patients.

items.question: How painful is stone treatment?
items.answer: Procedures are performed with anesthesia. Pain after treatment is usually manageable with medicines and improves quickly.

items.question: Can stones come back?
items.answer: Yes. Hydration, diet changes, metabolic tests, and follow-up plans reduce recurrence risk.

items.question: When is it an emergency?
items.answer: Fever, chills, uncontrolled pain, vomiting, pregnancy, a single kidney, or reduced urine output need urgent care.

items.question: How soon can I return to work?
items.answer: It depends on the treatment. Many patients return within a few days after ureteroscopy, while larger procedures may need longer rest.
